meta.inspection: All named milestone and landmark labels were read from 3x–4x enlarged crops of the complete 1026×1539 poster. No named label remained unreadable.
meta.decorativeIllustrations: Large unnamed silhouettes repeat named landmarks such as Statue of Liberty, Big Ben, Colosseum and Sydney Opera House. The generic Japanese castle/pagoda illustration above Jōmon is decorative and must not be assigned an invented building identity or prehistoric construction date.
meta.datePolicy: year is a convenient chronological anchor for a qualified development or construction phase, not a claim that all work occurred in one year. Null is used for uncertain prehistoric/cultural landscapes rather than inventing a founding date. Milestone numbers preserve the poster legend’s numbering.

milestones.note: Apollo 11 landed on 20 July UTC; the first steps followed on 21 July UTC. Earlier robotic lunar missions were uncrewed.
milestones.title: First crewed Moon landing

milestones.note: A long worldwide transition involving electronics, computers and networks, not a single national invention or founding date. The transistor of 1947 is one precursor.
milestones.title: Digital revolution

milestones.proposedTitle: Discovery and clinical use of insulin
milestones.note: The Toronto work involved Frederick Banting, Charles Best, J. J. R. Macleod and James Collip, alongside earlier international research; not the achievement of one person alone.
milestones.title: Discovery and clinical use of insulin

milestones.location: Southwestern Mexico, followed by wider American cultivation
milestones.note: A gradual Indigenous domestication process, not an invention by one later empire. Its beginning predates this timeline’s 3500 BC start.

sources.title: A perfect occasion to talk about domestication
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History

milestones.title: Maize domestication

milestones.dates: Developed across Preclassic, Classic and Postclassic Maya histories
milestones.note: No single invention date is justified. Maya observations, calendars and eclipse tables developed over centuries; surviving Dresden Codex astronomy reflects a later manuscript tradition.

sources.title: Maya Sun
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

milestones.title: Maya astronomy

milestones.location: Río de la Plata · Argentina and Uruguay
milestones.note: Developed in Buenos Aires and Montevideo from multiple cultural traditions. It belongs to both Argentina and Uruguay, rather than one country alone.
milestones.title: Tango

milestones.location: Australia and international research and standards networks
milestones.dates: 1992 · CSIRO WLAN breakthrough; Wi-Fi standards developed internationally
milestones.note: CSIRO’s Australian team made an important high-speed wireless LAN contribution. Wi-Fi as a whole involved many inventors, companies and IEEE standards; “Australia invented all Wi-Fi” overstates it.

sources.title: Bringing fast wireless connectivity to the world
CSIRO Wi-Fi invention selected for World in 100 Objects

milestones.title: Wireless LAN innovations and Wi-Fi

milestones.proposedTitle: Newton’s laws of motion and universal gravitation
milestones.note: Newton formulated these in the Principia, building on earlier mathematical and physical work. This is not the first human awareness of motion or gravity.
milestones.title: Newton’s laws of motion and universal gravitation

milestones.note: Watt greatly improved steam-engine efficiency; he did not invent the first steam engine. Newcomen and other predecessors must not disappear from the account.

sources.title: James Watt and the separate condenser

milestones.title: Watt’s separate condenser

milestones.location: Britain and research across multiple continents
milestones.dates: 1858 · Darwin–Wallace presentation; 1859 · On the Origin of Species
milestones.note: Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed explanations of natural selection and their work was jointly presented in 1858.
milestones.title: Evolution by natural selection

milestones.proposedTitle: Vasco da Gama’s sea voyage to India
milestones.wikiTitle: Portuguese discovery of the sea route to India
milestones.location: Portugal, Africa and the Indian Ocean
milestones.note: This opened a Portuguese Cape route to India, entering existing African, Arab, South Asian and other Indian Ocean trade networks. It was not the discovery of India or the first sea route there.
milestones.title: Vasco da Gama’s sea voyage to India

milestones.note: The Americas already had diverse Indigenous populations; Norse voyagers reached North America earlier. The label describes Columbus’s voyage and its consequences, rather than a universal “discovery.”
milestones.title: Columbus’s first Atlantic voyage

milestones.proposedTitle: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
milestones.wikiTitle: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
milestones.note: This French revolutionary declaration is a particular document, not the beginning of all rights traditions. Its stated universality coexisted with exclusions in political and colonial practice.

sources.title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

milestones.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

milestones.note: The French metric reforms and modern SI are related but not identical. SI was established in 1960 and continues to develop.

sources.title: Evolution of the SI
sources.publisher: Bureau International des Poids et Mesures

milestones.title: Development of the metric system

milestones.dates: c. 14th–17th centuries · dates vary by region
milestones.note: A broad cultural and intellectual period with regional variation, drawing on classical, Byzantine, Islamic and other knowledge transmissions; not one event or a universal historical stage.
milestones.title: European Renaissance

milestones.note: Gutenberg’s European metal-type system transformed European printing. Chinese woodblock printing and East Asian movable type preceded it by centuries.
milestones.title: Gutenberg’s movable-type printing system

milestones.dates: 1886 · Benz motor-car patent, among a longer development
milestones.note: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen is an early practical petrol automobile. Earlier steam road vehicles and parallel work by other inventors mean “first automobile” needs qualification.
milestones.title: The petrol automobile

milestones.location: Switzerland and Germany; wider scientific community
milestones.note: These are two connected theories, not a single publication. Einstein’s work developed within a wider mathematical and physical research community.

sources.title: Milestones of the theory of general relativity

milestones.title: Special and general relativity

milestones.proposedTitle: The Classical period in Western music
milestones.note: “Classical music” also names a much broader Western tradition. These dates refer to the Classical period associated with Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven, not all classical traditions worldwide.
milestones.title: The Classical period in Western music

milestones.dates: 776 BC · traditional first recorded ancient Games; 1896 · modern revival
milestones.note: 776 BC is the traditional recorded starting point, not proof that athletic festivals began then. Modern Olympic Games began in Athens in 1896.
milestones.title: Ancient and modern Olympic Games

milestones.dates: 508/507 BC · Cleisthenes’ reforms; further changes in the 5th century BC
milestones.note: Athenian democracy developed in stages. Political participation excluded women, enslaved people and resident foreigners; the date does not describe modern universal suffrage or every participatory tradition.
milestones.title: Development of Athenian democracy

milestones.note: The Code is one part of the wider Corpus Juris Civilis, alongside the Digest and Institutes and later Novels. It compiled and revised a long Roman legal tradition.

sources.title: Blume and Justinian: the Novels
sources.publisher: University of Wyoming College of Law

milestones.title: Justinian’s codification of Roman law

milestones.dates: From the 27th century BC · major Old Kingdom building
milestones.note: Djoser’s Step Pyramid precedes the great Giza pyramids. Pyramid-shaped monuments also arose in other societies; the poster’s Egyptian marker is not a universal beginning.

sources.title: The Step Pyramid Complex of Djoser
sources.publisher: Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities

milestones.title: Egyptian pyramid building

milestones.dates: 18th century BC · often dated c. 1750 BC
milestones.note: A major surviving Babylonian legal collection, not the world’s earliest law code. Earlier Mesopotamian legal collections survive.
milestones.title: Code of Hammurabi

milestones.dates: Ancient roots; documented traditions in the first millennium BC onward
milestones.note: Yoga developed across Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and other traditions. There is no agreed single origin date; interpreting Indus images as proof of modern yoga is uncertain.

sources.title: Yoga
sources.publisher: University of St Andrews Encyclopaedia of Theology

milestones.title: Yoga traditions

milestones.dates: Multiple developments; 628 AD · Brahmagupta’s arithmetic rules
milestones.note: Distinguish placeholder symbols from zero as an arithmetic number. Babylonian, Maya and South Asian developments cannot be reduced to a single inventor or place; 628 is an anchor for one important Indian text.

sources.title: The Maya
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

milestones.title: Zero: placeholders and a number

milestones.dates: Earlier Han-period evidence; 105 AD · traditional Cai Lun report
milestones.note: Cai Lun is traditionally credited with improving and reporting the process, not necessarily making the very first paper. Archaeological paper predates 105 AD.

sources.title: Cai Lun
sources.publisher: Hunan Provincial Department of Culture and Tourism

milestones.title: Papermaking in early China

milestones.dates: Earlier magnetic direction-finding; navigational use documented by the late 11th–early 12th centuries
milestones.note: Ancient lodestone direction-finding and medieval navigational compasses are distinct stages. The approximate year 1100 is an ordering anchor for documented Song-era navigation, not a single invention date.

sources.title: Sailing the Waters of East and Southeast Asia

milestones.title: Magnetic compasses and navigation

milestones.proposedTitle: Toyota Production System and lean manufacturing
milestones.dates: Mid-20th-century development; earlier roots and later international adoption
milestones.note: Toyota’s just-in-time and jidoka practices developed over decades and drew on earlier production ideas. “Lean” is a later term; no single invention year is adequate.
milestones.title: Toyota Production System and lean manufacturing

milestones.note: The Shinkansen opened a purpose-built high-speed passenger railway; this does not mean trains or high-speed experiments began in 1964.

sources.title: Shinkansen
sources.publisher: Embassy of Japan in the United Kingdom

milestones.title: Tōkaidō Shinkansen opens

landmarks.dates: 26th century BC
landmarks.note: The poster names the Great Pyramid; the linked complex includes the pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. These were built in the Old Kingdom, not at its opening boundary.
landmarks.title: Pyramids of Giza

landmarks.dates: From the Middle Kingdom, with major later additions
landmarks.note: A temple complex expanded over many reigns, especially in the New Kingdom, rather than one Middle Kingdom construction.
landmarks.title: Karnak temple complex

landmarks.dates: 13th century BC · reign of Ramesses II
landmarks.note: Ramesside rock-cut temples, relocated during the UNESCO Nubian monuments campaign in the 20th century.

sources.title: Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae

landmarks.title: Abu Simbel temples

landmarks.dates: c. 21st century BC, with later restorations
landmarks.note: Associated with Ur-Nammu and the Third Dynasty of Ur, not the entire loosely named “Sumerian Renaissance.”

sources.title: The Ahwar of Southern Iraq and Mesopotamian cities

landmarks.title: Great Ziggurat of Ur

landmarks.dates: c. 2600–1900 BC · mature urban phase
landmarks.note: The city belongs to the Mature Harappan phase. A poster placement near 3000 BC should not imply that every surviving structure dates to then.
landmarks.title: Mohenjo-daro

landmarks.note: An Elamite sacred complex built under Untash-Napirisha, not a monument constructed by later Iranian-speaking tribes.
landmarks.title: Chogha Zanbil

landmarks.dates: Multiple settlement phases · from the first millennium BC onward
landmarks.note: A serial archaeological landscape with different cities and Buddhist institutions, not one Vedic-period monument.
landmarks.title: Taxila archaeological sites

landmarks.dates: From c. 518 BC · Achaemenid construction
landmarks.note: Founded under Darius I and expanded by successors; damaged in Alexander’s conquest.
landmarks.title: Persepolis

landmarks.dates: Earlier regional walls; Qin linking c. 220 BC; major Ming work 1368–1644
landmarks.note: A network built and rebuilt across many periods. The familiar surviving brick sections are largely Ming, not all Zhou or Qin.
landmarks.title: Great Wall of China

landmarks.dates: Late 3rd century BC · First Qin Emperor’s mausoleum
landmarks.note: Belongs to the Qin imperial burial complex, not a Zhou-period monument.

sources.title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

landmarks.title: Terracotta Army

landmarks.dates: Bronze Age mining; cemetery principally c. 800–400 BC
landmarks.note: Hallstatt is an archaeological site and the name used for a broader material-culture period. The site’s long history should not be compressed into one culture-start date.
landmarks.title: Hallstatt salt mines and cemetery

landmarks.dates: Early 5th century BC dedication; later rebuilding
landmarks.note: Traditionally dedicated in 497 BC. The visible remains reflect later rebuilding; it was also associated with Rome’s treasury.

sources.title: Nel mezzo del Cammin: Temple of Saturn context

landmarks.title: Temple of Saturn

landmarks.dates: 447–432 BC · principal construction
landmarks.note: A Classical Athenian temple on the Acropolis, with a long subsequent history of religious use and transformation.
landmarks.title: Parthenon

landmarks.dates: Upper Palaeolithic · approximately 36,000–13,000 years ago
landmarks.note: The paintings predate the Celtic/Iberian societies beside which the poster places them. BP/years-ago dating must not be copied directly as BC; this site predates the chart’s range.

sources.title: Cave of Altamira and Paleolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain

landmarks.title: Cave of Altamira

landmarks.dates: Upper Palaeolithic · dating remains debated
landmarks.note: Not a monument built by Iron Age Gauls. Research has proposed different prehistoric dates; all are many millennia before 3500 BC and the chart’s range.
landmarks.title: Lascaux cave art

landmarks.dates: Neolithic and Bronze Age · principally 4th–3rd millennia BC
landmarks.note: Prehistoric megalithic tombs, not monuments constructed by the much later Lusitanian tribes beside which the poster places them.
landmarks.title: Antequera Dolmens

landmarks.dates: c. 3000 BC · earthwork; c. 2500 BC · principal stone setting
landmarks.note: Built long before the Celtic era. The poster’s Celtic attribution and late placement should be corrected, not reproduced.
landmarks.title: Stonehenge

landmarks.dates: c. 5th–13th centuries AD · multiple phases
landmarks.note: The monument icon’s placement high in the poster’s ancient column is not its construction date. Major flowering was much later than the earliest Maya communities.
landmarks.title: Chichén Itzá

landmarks.dates: c. 1st century BC–7th century AD · major urban phase
landmarks.note: The city predates the Mexica/Aztec Empire; later peoples named and revered its ruins.
landmarks.title: Teotihuacan archaeological city

landmarks.dates: Living Aṉangu cultural landscape · no single founding date
landmarks.note: A natural landform and sacred cultural landscape, not a constructed monument or a place founded around year 1. Aṉangu custodianship and Tjukurpa continue.
landmarks.title: Uluṟu cultural landscape

landmarks.dates: 70s–80 AD · initial construction and opening
landmarks.note: Built under the Flavian emperors; inaugurated in 80 AD and altered later.
landmarks.title: Colosseum

landmarks.dates: Developed from the early city through the Republic and Empire
landmarks.note: A civic and religious area with buildings of many dates. It is not a single building erected at the poster marker’s vertical position.
landmarks.title: Roman Forum

landmarks.dates: c. 600–1300 AD · principal Ancestral Pueblo occupation
landmarks.note: The celebrated cliff dwellings largely belong to the final centuries of this sequence. Living Pueblo communities maintain connections with these ancestral places.
landmarks.title: Mesa Verde Ancestral Pueblo sites

landmarks.dates: Used over approximately six millennia
landmarks.note: A communal bison-hunting landscape associated with Plains Indigenous peoples, especially Blackfoot histories. Its use long predates its low placement in the poster.
landmarks.title: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump

landmarks.dates: c. 850–1250 AD · major Chacoan building and influence
landmarks.note: Chaco is a network of Ancestral Pueblo places, connected to living Pueblo peoples; not a vanished single tribe.
landmarks.title: Chaco Culture archaeological sites

landmarks.dates: c. 900–1350 AD · major Mississippian centre
landmarks.note: A major Indigenous urban and ceremonial centre. Its significance must not be reduced to generic pre-US background.
landmarks.title: Cahokia Mounds

landmarks.dates: Traditional foundation 708; major abbey construction from the 10th century
landmarks.note: Its buildings span many centuries and should not be dated solely by the Frankish block in which the icon appears.
landmarks.title: Mont-Saint-Michel

landmarks.dates: 532–537 AD · Justinianic church
landmarks.note: The surviving main building is Justinianic, with earlier churches and later alterations; its religious use changed over time.
landmarks.title: Hagia Sophia

landmarks.dates: From c. 1070; rebuilt and enlarged over centuries
landmarks.note: Founded under William the Conqueror; it is not a single completed Norman building.
landmarks.title: Windsor Castle

landmarks.dates: From 1163 · principal medieval construction into the 14th century
landmarks.note: A Gothic cathedral with later restorations. The construction dates must be distinguished from modern reopening dates.
landmarks.title: Notre-Dame de Paris

landmarks.dates: Fortress from c. 1190; public museum inaugurated in 1793
landmarks.note: The poster places the museum in the medieval French kingdom, but the public museum opened during the Revolution. The medieval date belongs to the fortress.

sources.title: The Musée du Louvre at a glance

landmarks.title: Louvre palace and museum

landmarks.dates: 1173–14th century · interrupted construction
landmarks.note: The tower was built in medieval Pisa; its placement beside a later Sicilian kingdom must not imply that kingdom constructed it.
landmarks.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa

landmarks.dates: 1248–1880 · construction with a long interruption
landmarks.note: Started in the Holy Roman Empire and completed in the German Empire. It was not wholly constructed in one medieval period.
landmarks.title: Cologne Cathedral

landmarks.dates: 1147 · earlier church consecration; later Romanesque and Gothic building
landmarks.note: The current cathedral combines phases; substantial Gothic works date to the later Middle Ages.
landmarks.title: St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna

landmarks.dates: From the 13th century · major Nasrid palaces
landmarks.note: The Alhambra is associated principally with Nasrid Granada, rather than being a monument created by the Christian “Reconquista.”
landmarks.title: Alhambra

landmarks.dates: From 1501/1502 · principal 16th-century construction
landmarks.note: The foundation stone is dated to 1501 or 1502 in official accounts. Its 16th-century building should not be dated by its earlier vertical position in the poster.

sources.title: Monastery of the Hieronymites and Tower of Belém in Lisbon

landmarks.title: Jerónimos Monastery

landmarks.note: A fortified tower from the reign of Manuel I, not a 15th-century monument.

sources.title: Monastery of the Hieronymites and Tower of Belém in Lisbon

landmarks.title: Belém Tower

landmarks.dates: 1397 · villa origin; present pavilion rebuilt in 1955
landmarks.note: The Golden Pavilion is associated with Ashikaga Yoshimitsu. The present pavilion is a reconstruction following the 1950 fire.
landmarks.title: Kinkaku-ji

landmarks.dates: 1406–1420 · initial construction; later alterations
landmarks.note: Built under the Ming Yongle emperor and subsequently used and altered under Qing rule.

sources.title: Imperial Palaces of the Ming and Qing Dynasties

landmarks.title: Forbidden City

landmarks.note: An Ottoman mosque commissioned by Sultan Ahmed I; the familiar name refers to its blue interior tiles.
landmarks.title: Sultan Ahmed Mosque / Blue Mosque

landmarks.dates: Late 16th–early 17th century · Safavid transformation
landmarks.note: The square and its surrounding monuments developed under Safavid patronage, especially Shah Abbas I.
landmarks.title: Naqsh-e Jahan Square

landmarks.dates: 1632–1653 · mausoleum complex construction
landmarks.note: Commissioned by Shah Jahan in memory of Mumtaz Mahal; different parts of the complex were completed at different times.
landmarks.title: Taj Mahal

landmarks.dates: Earlier fortress; principal surviving complex c. 1601–1609
landmarks.note: The famous surviving castle is largely early Edo construction with earlier roots, rather than a single generic Tokugawa monument.
landmarks.title: Himeji Castle

landmarks.dates: Earlier hunting lodge; major expansion from 1661
landmarks.note: Versailles was expanded across several reigns. Louis XIV’s court moved there in 1682.
landmarks.title: Palace of Versailles

landmarks.dates: Late 17th–18th centuries · principal palace phases
landmarks.note: The present palace reflects Habsburg construction and major rebuilding, including Maria Theresa’s reign.
landmarks.title: Schönbrunn Palace

landmarks.dates: Construction from 1859; federal Parliament from 1867
landmarks.note: The original Centre Block was destroyed by fire in 1916 and rebuilt. The complex has several construction phases.
landmarks.title: Parliament Hill

landmarks.dates: 1886 · dedication
landmarks.note: A French-designed gift to the United States; its modern placement must not be read as an 18th-century independence-era construction.
landmarks.title: Statue of Liberty

landmarks.dates: 23 May 1936 · inauguration
landmarks.note: The monument commemorates the fourth centenary of the first Spanish foundation; it was not constructed at Argentine independence.
landmarks.title: Obelisco de Buenos Aires

landmarks.dates: 1859 · clock and Great Bell begin service
landmarks.note: Strictly, Big Ben is the Great Bell. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012; the familiar name is often used for the whole structure.

sources.title: A brief history of Big Ben and Elizabeth Tower

landmarks.title: Big Ben and Elizabeth Tower

landmarks.dates: 1887–1889 · construction
landmarks.note: Built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle; not a general marker for every French republic.

sources.title: History of the Eiffel Tower
sources.publisher: Société d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel

landmarks.title: Eiffel Tower

landmarks.dates: Construction began in 1882; continued across later eras
landmarks.note: The foundation predates Francoist Spain and modern constitutional Spain. No unsupported completion date should be inferred from the poster.
landmarks.title: Sagrada Família

landmarks.dates: 1959–1973 · principal construction; opened in 1973
landmarks.note: Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon with contributions by later teams; the cultural landmark is not evidence of one nation’s isolated invention.
landmarks.title: Sydney Opera House
